subtopic_detail: Frenotomy decision for ankyloglossia when the feeding problem is positional
stem:
You are the resident in a community paediatric clinic. A 9-day-old girl is brought in by her mother, who reports severe nipple pain through every feed and says the baby slips off the breast repeatedly and makes a clicking sound.

The baby was born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal delivery. Birth weight was 3400 g. Today she weighs 3250 g, which is above her day-4 nadir of 3100 g, and she has had six heavy nappies in the last 24 hours.

On examination the tongue elevates to the mid-mouth on crying and lateralises to both cheeks. A thin membrane runs from the undersurface of the tongue to a point just behind the lower gum ridge. The lactation consultant has observed a full feed and documented that the baby is held with her head well away from the breast and takes a shallow latch, and that nipple pain settles when the hold is changed.

data_table.Growth: Birth weight 3400 g, day-4 weight 3100 g, today 3250 g (regained above nadir)
data_table.Examination: Tongue elevates to mid-mouth, lateralises bilaterally, thin sublingual membrane inserting behind the lower gum ridge
data_table.Feeding assessment: Full breastfeed observed; shallow latch with head positioned away from the breast; pain settles with repositioning

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange structured lactation support with review of attachment and positioning in one week
options.rationale: Tongue elevation to mid-mouth with bilateral lateralisation and a membrane inserting behind the gum ridge is a mild restriction, and the observed pain resolved with repositioning, so the feeding problem is attachment rather than the frenulum. Weight has been regained above the nadir with adequate output, which buys time for hands-on lactation review before any procedure. (Source: RCH CPG: Breastfeeding problems)

options.text: Refer for frenotomy of the lingual frenulum to be performed within the next week
options.rationale: Frenotomy is reserved for restriction that demonstrably impairs feeding after skilled lactation assessment, and here the assessment identified a positional cause that responded to repositioning. Frenotomy would be correct if pain and transfer failed to improve with optimised attachment. (Source: RCH CPG: Breastfeeding problems)

options.text: Commence top-up feeds of infant formula after each breastfeed and review in one week
options.rationale: Weight is tracking up from the nadir with six heavy nappies daily, so intake is adequate and routine top-ups risk reducing maternal supply. Top-ups would be correct if weight were still falling or below the birth weight by day 14. (Source: RCH CPG: Breastfeeding problems)

options.text: Apply topical nystatin to the nipples and the baby's mouth and review in one week
options.rationale: Nipple and oral candidiasis causes persistent burning pain that does not change with repositioning, and there is no oral plaque or nipple appearance described here. Antifungal treatment would be correct if pain persisted after attachment was optimised and typical signs were present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer for division of an upper labial frenulum under general anaesthesia as a day case
options.rationale: Upper lip tie division has no established feeding benefit and the restriction described here is lingual, not labial. General anaesthesia is never the default route for a neonatal frenulum in any case, since frenotomy is an awake bedside procedure. (Source: RACGP: Tongue tie and breastfeeding)

explanation.summary: Nipple pain in the early weeks is far more often a problem of attachment and positioning than of anatomy, and the two are commonly conflated because a visible frenulum invites a mechanical explanation. Assessment of ankyloglossia is functional rather than anatomical: what matters is whether the tongue can elevate and lateralise enough to draw the nipple deep into the mouth, not whether a membrane is visible. A structured feed observation by a skilled practitioner is the investigation, and it frequently identifies a correctable hold. Frenotomy rates have risen internationally well beyond what the evidence supports, and an unnecessary procedure exposes a neonate to bleeding and to the false reassurance that the feeding problem has been addressed. Adequate output and a weight tracking up from the physiological nadir mean there is time to do this properly.
key_points: Tongue elevation to mid-mouth with bilateral lateralisation indicates mild restriction unlikely to be the cause of feeding failure
A full feed observed by a lactation practitioner is the assessment that decides whether a frenulum is functionally significant
Pain that settles with repositioning points to attachment rather than anatomy
Weight regained above the day-4 nadir with six or more heavy nappies daily indicates adequate transfer
Upper labial frenulum division has no established breastfeeding benefit
explanation.pearls: Physiological weight loss bottoms out around day 4 at up to 10 per cent of birth weight and birth weight should be regained by day 14; a baby already climbing from the nadir does not need top-ups while attachment is being corrected.

subtopic_detail: Radial head subluxation where the mechanism reported does not fit the classic pull
stem:
You are the resident in a suburban emergency department. A 3-year-old girl is brought in by her father because she will not use her left arm. He says she was swinging between him and her older sister by the hands when she suddenly cried out, and she has held the arm still against her body since.

She settled quickly and is now playing with a sticker using her right hand. She has no bruising anywhere and no previous fractures. Her father reports no fall and no direct blow.

On examination she holds the left arm slightly flexed at the elbow with the forearm turned palm-down. She resists turning the palm upward. There is no swelling, no deformity and no point tenderness over the clavicle, the humerus, the olecranon or the distal radius. She moves the fingers, wrist and shoulder normally and the radial pulse is present.

data_table.Examination: Left arm held flexed with forearm pronated, resists supination, no swelling or deformity, no point tenderness over clavicle, humerus, olecranon or distal radius, normal finger, wrist and shoulder movement, radial pulse present

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the elbow before attempting any manipulation
options.rationale: Radiographs are normal in radial head subluxation and delay a manoeuvre that restores function within minutes. Imaging would be correct if there were swelling, deformity, bony point tenderness or a mechanism involving a fall or direct blow. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

options.text: Perform a supination and flexion reduction manoeuvre at the bedside without prior imaging
options.rationale: A longitudinal traction mechanism with a pronated arm, absent swelling and no point tenderness over any bony landmark is a clinical diagnosis of radial head subluxation, and the management is immediate bedside reduction. Imaging before reduction is not required when the history and examination are typical and there is no localised bony tenderness. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

options.text: Apply an above-elbow backslab and arrange fracture clinic review within the following week
options.rationale: Immobilisation treats a fracture that has not been demonstrated and leaves a reducible subluxation unreduced for days. A backslab would be correct for a confirmed undisplaced supracondylar or forearm fracture, which would show swelling or focal tenderness. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

options.text: Perform a skeletal survey and notify the child protection team before any elbow manipulation
options.rationale: The mechanism is consistent, developmentally plausible and matches the injury, and there is no bruising or injury pattern raising concern. A skeletal survey would be correct where the history is absent, changes, or does not fit the injury, particularly in a child under 2 years. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Arrange an ultrasound of the elbow joint to exclude an effusion before attempting manipulation
options.rationale: Ultrasound is not part of the assessment pathway for a pulled elbow and an effusion is not the lesion in radial head subluxation. Ultrasound would be correct in suspected septic arthritis of the hip, where an effusion guides aspiration. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

explanation.summary: Radial head subluxation happens when the annular ligament slips over the radial head during axial traction on an extended, pronated arm, and it is one of the few paediatric musculoskeletal presentations diagnosed and cured within a single consultation. The classic picture is a child under 5 who simply stops using the arm rather than complaining of a specific painful point, which is why the absence of swelling and focal tenderness is as important as the mechanism. Reduction by supination with elbow flexion, or by hyperpronation, restores use within minutes and often produces a palpable click. Failure to regain use after two attempts is the trigger to image, because an undisplaced fracture can mimic the presentation. Recurrence is common until about age 5 and parents should be warned against lifting the child by the hands.
key_points: Axial traction on a pronated, extended arm is the mechanism; a fall or direct blow points elsewhere
The child refuses to use the arm rather than localising pain, and the arm is held pronated and slightly flexed
Absence of swelling, deformity and bony point tenderness makes imaging unnecessary before reduction
Supination with flexion or hyperpronation both work and often produce a palpable click
Image after two failed reduction attempts, because an occult fracture can present identically
explanation.pearls: Return of spontaneous arm use within about 15 minutes of a single supination and flexion manoeuvre confirms the diagnosis retrospectively; if the child is still not using the arm after two attempts, radiograph rather than repeat the manoeuvre a third time.

subtopic_detail: Referral threshold for persistent middle ear effusion with documented language delay
stem:
You are the resident in a general paediatric clinic. A 4-year-old boy is brought in by his mother because his preschool teacher says he does not respond when called from across the room and turns the television up loud.

He had two episodes of acute otitis media before his second birthday and none since. He has never had ear discharge and has no pain now. His mother says his speech is harder to understand than that of his younger cousins and that he uses short phrases rather than sentences.

On otoscopy both tympanic membranes are retracted and dull with visible fluid levels and no perforation. Tympanometry shows flat traces bilaterally. A formal audiogram today shows a bilateral conductive loss averaging 35 dB. A clinic note from a review 4 months ago documents the same otoscopic and tympanometric findings, and a speech pathology assessment 2 weeks ago placed his expressive language below the third centile for his age.

data_table.Examination: Both tympanic membranes retracted and dull with fluid levels, no perforation, no discharge
data_table.Investigations: Tympanometry flat bilaterally; audiogram bilateral conductive loss averaging 35 dB; identical otoscopic and tympanometric findings documented 4 months ago
data_table.Developmental: Speech pathology assessment 2 weeks ago: expressive language below the third centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue watchful waiting with a repeat audiogram and otoscopic review in a further 3 months
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is the correct approach for the first 3 months because most effusions resolve spontaneously, but that window has already passed and language is now measurably affected. Further observation would be correct if hearing were better than 25 dB and language were age-appropriate. (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion

options.text: Prescribe a 4-week course of oral amoxicillin and arrange otoscopic review at completion
options.rationale: Prolonged antibiotics do not produce durable resolution of a sterile middle ear effusion and expose the child to resistance and adverse effects. Amoxicillin would be correct for acute otitis media with a bulging erythematous drum and systemic symptoms, which are absent here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer to an ear, nose and throat surgeon for consideration of bilateral ventilation tube insertion
options.rationale: Bilateral effusion persisting beyond 3 months with a hearing loss of this degree and a documented language impact meets the threshold for surgical referral rather than further observation. The 4-month-old note establishes persistence, which is the element that converts watchful waiting into referral. (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion

options.text: Prescribe an intranasal corticosteroid spray for 8 weeks and arrange tympanometry at completion
options.rationale: Intranasal corticosteroids have not been shown to clear middle ear effusion or improve hearing outcomes in children. They would be correct for allergic rhinitis causing nasal obstruction, which is a separate problem and is not described here. (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion

options.text: Teach autoinflation with a nasal balloon device three times daily and review in 3 months
options.rationale: Autoinflation offers a small short-term benefit and is a reasonable adjunct during the observation window, but it does not substitute for referral once persistence and language impact are established. It would be correct as an interim measure in the first 3 months of a newly detected effusion. (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion

explanation.summary: Middle ear effusion after acute otitis media is extremely common and the great majority clears without intervention within 3 months, which is why the default is observation rather than treatment. The decision to operate turns on three things together: bilateral persistence beyond that window, the degree of hearing loss, and whether that loss is translating into a developmental or educational cost. A child with a 35 dB bilateral loss is missing conversational speech at a distance, and the speech pathology report converts an audiological number into a functional argument for intervention. Ventilation tubes restore hearing promptly and are usually extruded within 9 to 15 months. Antibiotics, steroids and decongestants have all been studied and none produces durable clearance, so offering them mainly delays the referral.
key_points: Observe for 3 months first: most effusions resolve spontaneously after acute otitis media
Refer when bilateral effusion persists beyond 3 months with hearing loss and a functional impact
A flat tympanogram with a retracted dull drum and fluid level confirms effusion rather than acute infection
Antibiotics, intranasal steroids and decongestants do not durably clear middle ear effusion
Document the developmental cost, since it is what converts an audiogram into an operative indication
explanation.pearls: A bilateral conductive loss averaging 25 dB or worse persisting past 3 months is the audiological trigger for ear, nose and throat referral; below that threshold, hearing is usually adequate for language acquisition and observation continues.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion
NICE: Otitis media with effusion in under 12s

subtopic_detail: Formula selection after a non-IgE cow milk reaction that recurred on an extensively hydrolysed feed
stem:
You are the resident in a paediatric outpatient clinic. A 10-week-old boy is brought in by his mother with 4 weeks of loose, mucousy stools streaked with blood and increasing irritability after feeds.

He has been formula fed since birth. Four weeks ago his general practitioner changed him from a standard cow milk formula to an extensively hydrolysed formula, which he has taken exclusively since. His mother reports the stools improved for about a week and then returned to being loose and blood-streaked.

He has never had hives, facial swelling, wheeze or vomiting within minutes of a feed. His weight has dropped from the 50th centile at birth to the 15th centile today. On examination he is alert and well perfused, the abdomen is soft and non-tender, and there is no perianal fissure, no skin rash and no organomegaly.

data_table.Examination: Alert, well perfused, abdomen soft and non-tender, no perianal fissure, no rash, no organomegaly
data_table.Feeding: Extensively hydrolysed formula exclusively for 4 weeks after standard cow milk formula; initial improvement then relapse

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Change to a soy based formula and arrange paediatric dietetic review within 2 weeks
options.rationale: A substantial proportion of infants with non-IgE cow milk proteinopathy react to soy as well, so soy is not a reliable next step under 6 months of age. Soy formula would be reasonable in an older infant with isolated IgE-mediated cow milk allergy and confirmed soy tolerance. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention

options.text: Request skin prick testing to cow milk protein and withhold any formula change pending results
options.rationale: Skin prick testing detects IgE sensitisation and is negative in the non-IgE delayed pattern described here, so a normal result would wrongly reassure. Testing would be correct if reactions occurred within minutes with urticaria, angioedema or wheeze. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention

options.text: Change to a lactose free cow milk formula and arrange paediatric dietetic review within 2 weeks
options.rationale: The reaction is to intact or partly hydrolysed cow milk protein, and a lactose free formula retains that protein while removing a sugar that is not the problem. Lactose free formula would be correct for transient secondary lactose intolerance after a proven gastroenteritis. (Source: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy

options.text: Change to an amino acid based formula and arrange paediatric dietetic review within 2 weeks
options.rationale: Persistent blood-streaked stools and centile fall despite 4 weeks of an extensively hydrolysed formula identify the minority of infants whose residual peptide load still drives the reaction, and the next step up the ladder is an amino acid based formula. Dietetic involvement is needed because faltering growth on an elimination diet requires energy and nutrient adequacy to be checked. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention

options.text: Request faecal calprotectin and colonoscopy and withhold any formula change pending results
options.rationale: Endoscopy is not required to diagnose food protein induced proctocolitis in a well infant, where response to elimination is the diagnostic test. Colonoscopy would be correct if bleeding persisted on an amino acid formula or if there were systemic features suggesting inflammatory bowel disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy

explanation.summary: Food protein induced allergic proctocolitis presents in the first months of life as blood-streaked mucousy stools in an otherwise well infant, and it is a delayed, non-IgE process, so allergy testing has no role in diagnosis. Management is a stepped elimination: an extensively hydrolysed formula first, which resolves the problem in roughly 90 per cent of cases, and an amino acid formula for the remainder who still react to residual peptides. The pattern of partial improvement followed by relapse on a hydrolysate is characteristic of that residual peptide load rather than of treatment failure through non-adherence. Faltering growth changes the urgency because it signals that intake and absorption are both being affected. Most infants tolerate cow milk protein again by 12 months, so a planned reintroduction under supervision belongs in the longer term plan.
key_points: Blood-streaked mucousy stools in a well infant suggest non-IgE food protein induced proctocolitis
Skin prick and specific IgE testing are negative in non-IgE disease and do not exclude it
Extensively hydrolysed formula is first-line and resolves about 90 per cent of cases
Amino acid formula is the next step when symptoms persist or relapse on a hydrolysate
Soy formula is unsuitable under 6 months because of frequent co-reactivity
explanation.pearls: Expect symptoms to settle within 2 to 4 weeks of starting an appropriate elimination formula; relapse after an initial week of improvement on an extensively hydrolysed feed is the signal to escalate to amino acid based formula rather than to question adherence.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention
RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing positional head flattening from suture fusion in an infant with a ridged head shape
stem:
You are the resident in a community child health clinic. A 5-month-old boy is brought in by his father because the back of his head looks flat and one ear looks pushed forward.

He was born at term and sleeps on his back. His father says he has always preferred to turn his head to the right and that he spends most of his waking time in a bouncer. Head circumference has tracked along the 50th centile since birth.

On examination the right occiput is flattened, the right ear sits anterior to the left and the right forehead is more prominent than the left, so that the head viewed from above is a parallelogram. The anterior fontanelle is open and soft. There is no palpable ridge over any suture. Passive neck rotation is restricted to the left with a firm thickening palpable in the right sternocleidomastoid.

data_table.Growth: Head circumference on the 50th centile since birth
data_table.Examination: Right occipital flattening with right ear anterior and right frontal bossing, parallelogram head shape from above, anterior fontanelle open and soft, no palpable sutural ridge
data_table.Neck: Passive rotation restricted to the left, firm thickening palpable in the right sternocleidomastoid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to a craniofacial surgeon for assessment of premature fusion of the lambdoid suture
options.rationale: Lambdoid synostosis produces a trapezoid head with the ipsilateral ear displaced posteriorly and a palpable ridge, which is the opposite ear displacement to the parallelogram described here. Referral would be correct if the ear sat posteriorly, a ridge were palpable, or head circumference were crossing centiles. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

options.text: Request a computed tomography scan of the skull with three-dimensional reconstruction of the sutures
options.rationale: Positional plagiocephaly is a clinical diagnosis and computed tomography delivers ionising radiation to an infant brain for no management gain. It would be correct where examination genuinely suggests synostosis and a craniofacial service requests it to plan surgery. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

options.text: Arrange fitting of a moulding helmet orthosis now and review the head shape in 3 months
options.rationale: Helmet therapy is a second-line option considered from around 6 months when conservative measures have failed, and it does nothing for the underlying neck restriction. It would be correct for severe persisting asymmetry after an adequate trial of physiotherapy and repositioning. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

options.text: Advise front sleeping overnight to offload the flattened occiput and review the head shape in 3 months
options.rationale: Prone sleeping is a major modifiable risk factor for sudden unexpected death in infancy and must never be advised to improve head shape. Repositioning is achieved by alternating head orientation while supine and by waking tummy time under supervision. (Source: Red Nose Australia: Safe sleeping)

options.text: Refer to physiotherapy for neck stretching and advise repositioning and supervised tummy time
options.rationale: A parallelogram head shape with the ipsilateral ear displaced anteriorly, a normal head circumference and no sutural ridge is positional deformity driven by a restricted sternocleidomastoid, and the treatment is physiotherapy for the torticollis plus repositioning. Treating the neck restriction is the element that prevents recurrence, because the head shape follows the preferred head position. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

explanation.summary: Positional plagiocephaly became substantially more common after supine sleeping was adopted to reduce sudden unexpected death in infancy, and it is benign, but it is frequently confused with craniosynostosis. The discriminator is geometry rather than severity: positional flattening pushes the ipsilateral ear and forehead forward, producing a parallelogram viewed from above, while lambdoid synostosis restricts growth and pulls the ipsilateral ear backward into a trapezoid with a palpable ridge. Congenital muscular torticollis underlies a large share of positional cases and is the reason the deformity recurs if only repositioning is advised. Head circumference crossing centiles or a ridged suture are the findings that should prompt craniofacial referral. Most positional asymmetry improves substantially once the infant becomes mobile and spends less time lying against a surface.
key_points: Parallelogram head with the ipsilateral ear displaced anteriorly indicates positional deformity
Trapezoid head with the ipsilateral ear displaced posteriorly plus a palpable ridge indicates lambdoid synostosis
Normal head circumference tracking along a centile argues against synostosis
Treat the associated sternocleidomastoid restriction or the head shape will recur
Never advise prone sleeping to offload a flattened occiput
explanation.pearls: Check passive neck rotation in every infant with an asymmetric head: congenital muscular torticollis drives the positional preference, and physiotherapy started before 6 months resolves the great majority without a helmet.
